title: Why I Stopped Asking What Are You Working On
author: Rod Naquin
summary: An instructional coach reconsiders a question he had asked in every coaching conversation of his career, "what are you working on?", after finding it produced a misleadingly fixed label ("academic feedback") rather than a live diagnosis of what a student teacher actually needed. Drawing on Mary Kennedy's research, he reframes teaching not as a set of discrete skills mastered once, but as five persistent problems that resurface differently in every class period. Observing the same teacher across two periods revealed two entirely different underlying challenges hiding under one coaching label. The piece then brings in organizational paradox theory from Smith and Lewis to explain why some classroom tensions, like opening up participation while maintaining behavior, can't be permanently solved, only managed through continuous, deliberate oscillation. The author proposes a replacement coaching question that asks which persistent problem is alive in a specific room, on a specific day.
points: Mary Kennedy's research reframes teaching not as a set of discrete skills to master once, but as five persistent problems (content, participation, exposing thinking, behavior, teacher needs) that resurface differently in every class period.

A single coaching label like "academic feedback" can mask two entirely different underlying problems in two different class periods, so effective coaching has to diagnose room by room, not skill by skill.

Organizational paradox theory (Smith & Lewis) explains why some classroom tensions — like opening up participation versus maintaining behavior — can't be permanently resolved, only managed through continuous oscillation.
Reframing a recurring struggle as a paradox rather than a failure changes the coaching conversation from "fix this" to "lean this direction on purpose, then check the other pole."
quotes: It's the kind of answer that sounds like a goal but is really a label, a single named deficit meant to travel with her from lesson to lesson, room to room, as if it were a fixed skill she either has or doesn't.

She argues teaching isn't organized around discrete skills you build once and carry forward, but around five persistent problems that never fully resolve and show up differently depending on the room.

Third period was a participation problem - getting quieter kids into the actual thinking. Fourth period was a behavior-and-participation trade-off - it was hard to open discussion up without losing the room, which meant there was barely any thinking to feed back on in the first place.

Some tensions are paradoxes - two things that are both true and both necessary, permanently, where pushing hard on one pole makes the other pole scream louder. You don't resolve a paradox by picking a winner.
Once we named it that way, the goal for each room stopped being "fix this" and became "lean this direction on purpose, knowing we'll check the other side again soon.

Instead of asking what someone is working on as a single standing goal, ask which of the persistent problems of teaching feels most alive in a specific class, on a specific day - then ask whether it's a one-time fix or a tension you'll be leaning through all semester.
